name: Holy Rollers
label: Dischord
lede: A DC punk trio that did the one thing nobody in the Dischord basement was doing in 1989: they all sang, at once, in harmony.

eras.title: Three voices in a church basement
eras.text: DC hardcore had one singer and a lot of shouting. Holy Rollers split the mic three ways, pulled from no wave, LA hardcore and first-wave punk, and started their life on a bill with Fugazi, the band everyone in town was watching.

years.h: Holy Rollers: a trio where everybody sings
years.p: Marc Lambiotte on guitar, Joe Aronstamn on bass, Maria Jones on drums, all three on vocals. Wikipedia calls them the first DC punk band to work in three-part harmony; Dischord says among the first.

years.h: Holy Rollers' first show: opening for [[Fugazi|233fc3f3-6de2-465c-985e-e721dbabbace]] at the Wilson Center
years.p: Holy Rollers debut in the Wilson Center, a hall in the basement of a former Mount Pleasant church, opening a bill of Fugazi, [[Swiz|eea2f3d8-1e94-436c-ae66-4633f99f55be]] and Edsel, per Wikipedia.
years.xp: The Wilson Center was the default all-ages room of that era of DC punk, a church basement where Positive Force benefits and Dischord bands turned over week after week. Dischord's own history of the band opens right there, with the Holy Rollers going on first and Fugazi, barely a year old, headlining.

years.h: Holy Rollers' first EP, The Origami Sessions
years.p: Holy Rollers' first recording, which Wikipedia credits to Dischord and Adult Swim Records. It isn't in Dischord's own catalog listing for the band.

eras.title: Harmonies in a hardcore town
eras.text: In the politically charged DC underground of the early '90s, Dischord calls Holy Rollers one of the more active bands going. Two albums in two years, songs about DC street life and being broke, and a studio door always open to guests.

years.p: Holy Rollers' debut album. Trouser Press heard a band with a remarkable range of musical knowledge and real enthusiasm for punk-rock variety, even where the playing couldn't keep up with the ideas.

years.h: "Eleventy" and "What You Said" at the 9:30 Club, March 3, 1990
yt: "Eleventy" and "What You Said" at the 9:30 Club, March 3, 1990

q: Fugazi filtered through the Soft Boys.
years.p: Ten songs, from Changeling to the title track, still the classic trio. Trouser Press notes a guest turn from [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]].
years.xp: Dischord paired it with the debut on a single CD, Fabuley + As Is (No. 59), which is how most people outside DC first heard them. The band also brought in spoken-word artist Juliana Luecking and a rotating cast of guest musicians, something Dischord's bio singles out.

years.p: Out on Shred of Dignity Records, per Wikipedia, a sideways step off Dischord for a shared single.

eras.title: Richmond reinforcements
eras.text: Losing a drummer usually ends a trio. Holy Rollers instead turned into a four-piece with two Richmond players, a second guitar and a harder, plainer sound, and kept going until 1995.

years.h: Maria Jones leaves for San Francisco; [[Ed Trask|0cf5525b-a45c-4e1d-b269-d306b793d442]] takes the drums
years.p: Dischord says drummer Maria Jones left for San Francisco and was replaced by Ed Trask from Richmond, Virginia, later known back home as a painter of big public murals. Wikipedia says Jones joined queercore band [[Tribe 8|10df0f02-bd7c-4193-91aa-dc3222e0f37d]].

years.h: [[Chris Maynard Bopst|e258b83f-947f-466a-a75b-9d26fda2f1e3]] on bass makes Holy Rollers a four-piece
years.p: Chris Maynard Bopst takes over bass and Joe Aronstamn moves to second guitar. With Ed Trask on drums, the rhythm section is all Richmond.
A single ahead of the band's self-titled third album.
Recorded at Inner Ear with John Morand producing. Trouser Press thought the new line-up narrowed its vision toward tried and true DC rock and pulled back on the vocal intricacy.

years.h: Holy Rollers break up after six years
years.p: Holy Rollers call it quits. Dischord's listing gives the active run as winter 1989 to 1995.

eras.title: Positive Force calls them back
eras.text: Thirty years on, the benefit-show collective that shaped their scene turned 40 and asked the old bands to play. Holy Rollers said yes and didn't stop at one night.

years.h: Holy Rollers reunite for Positive Force at 40
years.p: Marc Lambiotte, Joe Aronstamn and Ed Trask reunite for the activist group's 40th anniversary, a five-day run of shows and protests that also brought back [[Swiz|eea2f3d8-1e94-436c-ae66-4633f99f55be]], who had shared their very first bill.

years.h: Holy Rollers headline the Black Cat with a new bassist
years.p: With [[Graham McCulloch|a9cb94ec-b297-44d5-9ea1-dbefe4b26c33]] joining on bass in 2026, Holy Rollers headline D.C.'s Black Cat with [[Hammered Hulls|64368968-d520-49ea-a248-9ccc29e1467f]] and The Owners.
